Please read this carefully:

<document>
# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

response:
This is a much stronger piece of work than the Halden pilot. It has:

- randomisation stratified by the variable that matters most (whether output depends on staff being present)
- output taken from administrative records and hours from timesheets
- a registered primary outcome, with clustered standard errors
- an exploratory analysis that is clearly labelled and properly hedged
- an explicit statement of why per-scheduled-hour figures mislead

It answers most of the problems I raised about the Halden paper, and its results point the same way: per-hour gains are overstated by the scheduled-hours convention, and coverage-bound work behaves differently.

The arithmetic checks out. Case-processing: 0.979 / 0.87 = +12.5%, or +22% against scheduled hours. Counter: 0.886 / 0.83 = +6.7%. The hours figures (37.9→33.0, 37.6→31.2) match the stated 13% and 17%.

The remaining issues are real but mostly second-order. I've grouped them by how much they could change the conclusions.

## Could change the conclusions

**1. Sick days may fall partly by construction.** The paper doesn't say whether the 30-hour rota means shorter days or fewer days. If staff work four days instead of five, there are about 20% fewer days on which to be absent, and sick days per FTE would fall by roughly that amount with no change in health. The −29% should be reported per scheduled day or hour. On a per-day basis, the true effect could be much smaller than it looks. The same issue applied to the Halden figures.

**2. Case-processing output was partly bought with paid overtime.** Actual hours fell by only 13% "reflecting overtime claimed." So treated offices paid full salary for 30 hours plus overtime, while output per FTE was −2.1%. Cost per case closed almost certainly rose. The Discussion says per-hour gains don't imply the reduction "pays for itself" only about counter offices, but it also applies to case-processing. A cost-per-output figure would make this concrete.

**3. Timesheets only record overtime that was claimed.** Unpaid work, such as finishing a case after clocking off or checking email on the day off, wouldn't appear. Missing hours would inflate the 12.5% figure. That is the same kind of overstatement the paper rightly criticises in scheduled-hours estimates, just smaller. Even a short time-use survey of a subsample would help bound it.

**4. "Little or no measurable loss" is not the same as no loss.** The case-processing interval (−6.8 to +2.6) cannot rule out a loss of about 7%. "Statistically indistinguishable from control" is accurate. "Little or no loss" reads as a claim of equivalence that the trial wasn't powered to make. If the county has a tolerable loss in mind, say 3%, an equivalence test against it would answer the policy question directly.

## Design and inference

**5. Too few clusters for standard clustered errors.** The counter stratum has 5 v 5 offices and the case stratum 7 v 7. Conventional cluster-robust standard errors are biased downward with this few clusters. The counter per-hour interval (+0.4 to +13.3) only just excludes zero and could include it under a correction. Wild cluster bootstrap or randomisation inference would be more defensible. The latter is especially natural, since the randomisation scheme is known.

**6. Test the difference between strata directly.** The headline is that the effect "differed sharply by type of work." That needs an interaction test, not two separate intervals. The intervals overlap slightly (−6.8 to −5.9). A rough calculation suggests the difference of about 9 points is probably significant, but it should be reported. The paper should also state whether stratum-specific estimates were the registered primary analysis or whether a pooled estimate was registered first. If pooled, it should be reported.

**7. Interference between offices, especially counters and phone lines.** Treated counters had longer waits and more abandoned calls. Did some of that demand move to control offices, through members of the public going elsewhere or shared call routing? If so, control output rose because treated output fell, and the difference-in-differences double-counts the effect. That would make the −11.4% too large. If the counties' contact centres share a phone queue, that needs addressing explicitly.

**8. Some service outcomes aren't analysed with the trial's design.**
- Waiting time and abandoned calls are reported only as treated offices before and after, with no control comparison.
- Quality outcomes (3.1% v 3.0%, 11.8% v 10.9%) appear to be month-9 levels, not difference-in-differences estimates, and have no intervals.
- The rise in counter repeat contacts (+0.9 points) isn't discussed. It may be noise, but it points the same way as the waits.

These should all be estimated as difference-in-differences with intervals, as the primary outcome is.

## Interpretation

**9. The counter per-hour gain may be queueing arithmetic, not effort.** With fewer staff present during unchanged opening hours, each staff member spends less time idle between contacts. Contacts per hour rise because the queue is longer, and the public bears the cost in waiting time. "Each hour worked was somewhat more productive" assumes rest or effort as the explanation. Higher utilisation explains it equally well, and that matters for anyone trying to extrapolate. Comparing handling time per contact with time spent idle would distinguish the two.

**10. Case-processing output may hide changes in case mix or a growing backlog.** "Cases closed" over nine months could stay flat while staff close easier cases first and let harder ones age within statutory deadlines. The Limitations section raises backlog risk, but backlog size and the age profile of open cases are already in the case-management system and could be reported now, along with a measure of case complexity if one exists.

**11. Meetings: there is no pre-period.** Meeting time was measured only in month six. The 3.3-hour gap is therefore a difference in level, not a change, and part of it could predate the trial. The other caveats are already handled well: unregistered analysis, seven offices, correlation is not mechanism. For reference, r = 0.71 with n = 7 has p ≈ 0.07 and a confidence interval running from about zero to 0.95. Pulling pre-period calendar data, if it exists, would strengthen the analysis more than anything else in this section. Registering the confirmatory test is the right move.

**12. Control offices may have reacted to the trial.** The Limitations section covers effort. Staff who know colleagues elsewhere are getting a shorter week may also resign or take sick leave more out of resentment. That would inflate the resignation and sick-day gaps. It's worth a sentence, and checking control offices' trends against their own pre-period would show whether it happened.

## Minor

- State how FTE is defined after treatment. Presumably a 30-hour employee still counts as 1.0 FTE, but it should be explicit.
- Sick days and resignations need intervals. The resignation caveat is good; the sick-day figure is presented with more confidence than its precision supports.
- The final paragraph of the Discussion, on what matters being whether a role's output depends on presence rather than which sector it is in, is the most useful generalisable point in the paper. It could be in the Summary.

## Overall

The main conclusions look robust:
- Scheduled-hours estimates overstate per-hour gains.
- Coverage-bound work loses output and service quality.
- Per-hour and per-employee productivity diverge.

The parts most likely to shrink under scrutiny are:
- the sick-day effect, if part of it comes from fewer working days;
- the case-processing per-hour gain, once overtime costs and unrecorded hours are included;
- the counter per-hour gain, if it reflects busier queues rather than greater effort.

None of these overturns the paper. Several can be checked with data the county already holds.
